summary:
Junior Astronaut 3D is a free 3D browser game in which children aged 7–12 run a small Mars outpost for six sols. It works on phones and computers, in English and Mongolian, with no install or account.

Kids learn engineering trade-offs by living them. Three machines (oxygen, water, food) share one power budget, so the player chooses what runs. Materials must be collected outside, where suit oxygen drops and the crew's radiation dose builds up. Every emergency offers a careful plan and a quick plan, and neither is free. Asking Earth for advice takes a realistic light-time delay while the problem keeps running, which shows why Mars crews must decide for themselves.

Real NASA data drives the game: each game's solar flare is the strongest one in NASA's DONKI database from the last 30 days (a real 2024 flare when offline), the radiation dose is based on Curiosity RAD measurements, and the greenhouse cites NASA OSDR research on lettuce grown on the ISS. A real astronaut story follows every emergency, a failure report explains each lost heart, and a read-aloud button helps young readers. Every game is different, so kids want to play again.
details:
WHAT IT IS

Junior Astronaut 3D is a 3D browser game for children aged 7–12. The player commands a small Mars outpost and must keep the crew alive for six sols (Martian days) until a supply ship lands. It runs in any modern browser on phones and computers, needs no install or account, works offline after loading, and is available in English and Mongolian.

Play: https://lucky-mars.vercel.app

Code: https://github.com/azaanm7/LUCKY

HOW IT WORKS: THREE CORE SYSTEMS

• Life support: an oxygen maker, a water recycler and a greenhouse keep the air, water and food bars up. Each needs power and a material: printed filters, melted ice, seeds and water.

• Power: solar panels and one battery feed every machine. The sun cannot run all three machines all day and still charge the battery for the night, so the player decides what to switch off. When power runs short, every machine slows down together. Dust storms cut solar power, and the panels must be wiped clean by hand.

• Radiation: the crew's dose rises fast outside, slowly in the shelter and sharply during a solar flare, and it never goes down, so every trip outside has a lasting cost.

To get materials, the player explores the surface for ice, ore and seed crates. The backpack holds six items, so every trip is a choice between survival materials and science samples. A 3D printer in the workshop turns ore into spare parts and upgrades, using the same power budget.

NO CHOICE IS FREE

From sol 2, every sol brings an emergency that real astronauts have faced, in a different order each game: a clogged CO₂ filter (Apollo 13), a dust storm (Opportunity rover, 2018), a solar flare (Orion's radiation shelter plan), an air leak through a tiny hole (the 2 mm hole sealed on the ISS in 2018) and a failing water pump (ISS water recycling). Each card offers a careful plan that takes time and a quick plan with a lasting cost. A third button asks Earth for advice: the answer takes a realistic Mars light-time delay (6–20 minutes, compressed to 4–15 seconds) while the emergency keeps running, and during a solar flare it arrives too late. Afterwards the player reads how real astronauts solved the same problem and earns a badge.

REAL NASA DATA, SHOWN IN THE GAME

• NASA DONKI (live): when the game opens, it requests the last 30 days of solar flares from NASA's DONKI space weather database and uses the strongest one as this game's flare. Its class sets how much radiation it adds and how likely it is to damage a running machine. For example, an M3.5 flare (5 Nov 2026) adds about 19 dose points in an unshielded shelter and has a 23% chance of damaging a machine if the shield stays off, while the archived X9.0 flare (3 Oct 2024) adds about 81 points with a 90% chance. Without internet, the game uses eight real 2024 flares and says on screen that it is using the archive; it never labels archived data as live.

• Curiosity RAD: the base dose rate is the 0.64 mSv per day that Curiosity's RAD instrument measured on the surface of Mars (Hassler et al., Science 2014), scaled for the game.

• NASA OSDR (study OSD-268): the greenhouse fact comes from the Veggie lettuce grown on the ISS, which scientists tested for germs that make people sick (none were found); the crew ate part of the crop.

• NASA mission facts (MOXIE, Opportunity, Orion, Veggie, ISS 3D printing) explain each machine and event.

A "Science and sources" page inside the game links every source and states plainly that consumption and production rates are tuned for play and are not real mission values.

LEARNING WITHOUT READING RULES

• The first sol is a training sol: six actions, each with a guide arrow.

• One prompt line always shows the most urgent task.

• A read-aloud button reads the cards and prompts with the device's own voice.

• At the end, a failure report traces each lost heart to its cause (for example: dust storm → dusty panels → not enough power → oxygen ran out), gives one tip and explains what an engineering trade-off is.

IMPACT

Space STEM content for kids is usually either oversimplified or too complex. Here, kids feel the same trade-offs that mission planners face (power vs. life support, speed vs. safety, science vs. risk) and learn that every decision has a cost. Our balance tests show that strategy matters: in 300 automated games per strategy, a player who does nothing never wins, a player who manages power wins about 81% of games, and only players who also take science risks earn extra stars. Every game is different (shuffled emergencies, the current real flare, three stars to chase), so kids want to play again. Because it is free, phone-friendly, bilingual and works offline, it suits classrooms with limited computers or internet, including in Mongolia.

HOW WE BUILT IT

TypeScript, React 19, three.js (3D), Tailwind CSS 4, Vite and Bun. Web Audio API for sound effects and background music generated in code (no audio files); Web Speech API for read-aloud. Hosted on Vercel; GitHub Actions run 94 automated tests, lint and build on every change, and a failing test blocks the deploy. The game logic is a pure, tested engine kept separate from the 3D renderer, and balance bots play hundreds of games so that any change that breaks the learning goal fails the tests. The renderer lowers its quality automatically on weak devices.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

• Age: short sentences (checked automatically), pixel icons, simple controls (keyboard or touch joystick).

• Honesty: real data is labeled live or archive, and game numbers are labeled as game rules.

• Access and privacy: no account and no tracking; the only data request goes to NASA DONKI, and the game works offline.

• Space Apps rules: no NASA logos or branding.

USE OF AI

AI coding assistants (Claude and Claude Code by Anthropic) helped write code, tests and documentation from our own game design; we reviewed and tested every change. The pixel icons, the app icon and the background music were made in code with AI assistance. Every AI-assisted change is logged in docs/AI_USAGE.md in our repository.
